items.title: Domain-Driven Design for AI Agents: Contexts and Rules
items.summary:
# Domain-Driven Design for AI Agents: Contexts and Rules

This guide is for Python engineers building AI agents that change business data. You will learn how Domain-Driven Design (DDD) organizes business vocabulary and rules, and how to turn a model proposal into an authorized operation.

Agent projects become difficult to change when prompts, code, and business processes use different terms. Compliance asks for a "policy check," while the implementation exposes `process_data()`. The vague name hides which rule is being applied, who owns it, and where a change belongs.

DDD puts that business language and ownership at the center. The language model interprets a request and proposes an operation with named, typed fields. Application code supplies trusted user information, checks permission, and invokes the business rules before saving a change.

items.title: Schema-Guided Reasoning: vLLM, XGrammar, and Pydantic
items.summary:
# Schema-Guided Reasoning: vLLM, XGrammar, and Pydantic

This article is for Python engineers who need model output that downstream code can validate. You will learn how to define a Pydantic schema, request structured output from vLLM, and add application checks for meaning and policy.

Pydantic describes the response fields, vLLM serves the model, and XGrammar restricts which tokens the model can generate. This restriction is called constrained decoding. It applies only the schema features supported by the decoding backend, here XGrammar. A token limit can still leave an incomplete JSON prefix, so application code must check completion and validate the result.

items.title: LLM Fine-Tuning Guide: LoRA, QLoRA, Unsloth, Axolotl
items.summary:
# LLM Fine-Tuning Guide: LoRA, QLoRA, Unsloth, Axolotl

This guide is for Python engineers deciding whether and how to fine-tune a large language model. You will learn when to choose fine-tuning over prompting or retrieval and how to choose between methods such as LoRA and QLoRA. The guide also explains how to prepare data, evaluate the trained model, and plan its deployment.

The examples explain configurations and checks. They are not a verified end-to-end training recipe; the practical section separates the companion repository commands from a proposed training configuration.

items.title: AI Agent Reasoning Loops: ReAct, ReWOO, Plan-and-Execute
items.summary:
# AI Agent Reasoning Loops: ReAct, ReWOO, Plan-and-Execute

An **agent reasoning loop** is the control flow that decides when a model plans, calls a tool, reads the result, and stops. This article helps engineers building agents choose between **ReAct**, **ReWOO**, and **Plan-and-Execute** and implement each pattern in LangGraph. You will learn how that choice changes model-call count, the history each call carries, and whether a surprising result can change the next action.

The examples use a LangGraph Market Analyst Agent I built, with a router that selects a pattern for each request.

The loop is the innermost layer of the series. Memory, tools, security, runtime, and checks before a task is declared done surround it; they do not replace it.

items.title: Search Ranking Stack: BM25, Embeddings, and Reranking
items.summary:
# Search Ranking Stack: BM25, Embeddings, and Reranking

This guide is for Python engineers building or improving a search ranking pipeline. It explains how BM25, dense embeddings, rank fusion, and rerankers work together, and how to measure whether search needs better candidates or a better order.

A search for "cheap laptop" can miss a product described as a "budget notebook computer." A different failure puts a headphone carrying case above the headphones themselves. The first problem needs better candidates; the second needs a better order. The [companion demo repository](https://github.com/slavadubrov/search-ranking-stack) illustrates retrieval and reranking on a sampled slice of Amazon ESCI product-search data.

items.title: AI Agent Memory Architecture: Checkpoints and Vector Stores
items.summary:
# AI Agent Memory Architecture: Checkpoints and Vector Stores

This guide is for engineers building AI agents that must carry progress and knowledge across requests and restarts. You will learn where to use checkpoints for recovery, structured or vector stores for recall, and files for project knowledge.

Without stored state, an agent cannot resume a paused plan, recover after a crash, or recall a preference from an earlier conversation. [Part 1](/blog/2026/01/31/ai-agent-reasoning-loops/) covered the reasoning loop that chooses and executes actions. Here, the question is which state each later turn needs and where that state should live.

I'll use the [Market Analyst Agent](https://github.com/slavadubrov/market-analyst-agent) — a small LangGraph agent that fetches market data and writes an analyst report — to anchor the hot-checkpoint discussion. The cold-vector and raw-Markdown sections are independent illustrative designs that show extensions the current project does not yet implement. Then I'll cover when PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, key-value stores, and plain Markdown files each make sense.

items.title: Data Processing Engines: Polars, DataFusion, Ray, and Spark
items.summary:
# Data Processing Engines: Polars, DataFusion, Ray, and Spark

This guide helps Python and data engineers choose a processing engine for tabular data and image, audio, or text pipelines. It explains how Polars, DataFusion, Daft, Ray Data, and Spark execute work, which workloads suit them, and how to compare them on your own data.

Modern pipelines also process images, audio, and video. In these workloads, CPU decoding can starve GPU inference. Native operators, columnar data exchange, and overlapping CPU/GPU work address different costs; choosing an engine means finding which cost limits your pipeline.

To compare the options, I benchmarked Pandas, Polars, DataFusion, Daft, and native Rust on two real datasets. Spark and Ray are covered in separate distributed notebooks. NYC taxi trips represent tabular work; Food-101 images represent a multimodal pipeline.

The [engine-comparison-demo repository](https://github.com/slavadubrov/engine-comparison-demo) contains the code. The historical runs below have unequal timing or processing scopes, so use them to design a fair test on your own hardware. The code examples are API sketches: they require the named libraries, input files, and storage access; GPU examples also need the model weights and CUDA workers. They illustrate the APIs rather than reproduce the recorded timings.

items.title: OCR in 2026: Classical Pipelines, VLMs, and Document AI
items.summary:
# OCR in 2026: Classical Pipelines, VLMs, and Document AI

This guide is for engineers choosing OCR and document extraction for search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or AI agents. It explains how traditional engines and vision-language models differ, how to evaluate text, tables, and fields, and how to route difficult documents to another model or human review.

Vision-language models (VLMs) can handle layout, handwriting, tables, and degraded images that break a plain text-recognition pipeline. Traditional engines remain competitive on clean print, especially when CPU latency and operating cost matter. The dated snapshot below includes [PaddleOCR-VL 1.6](https://www.paddleocr.ai/main/en/version3.x/pipeline_usage/PaddleOCR-VL.html) and [dots.mocr](https://github.com/rednote-hilab/dots.mocr), with different hardware, privacy, and output trade-offs. Check each project before making a current choice.

> **Companion repo:** [**The OCR Gauntlet**](https://github.com/slavadubrov/ocr-gauntlet/tree/deb94ebd747f0e7cc14b523ac3d0ad19032f855a) contains three instructional notebooks and five downloaded samples at this pinned revision. It is a smoke demo, not a validated engine ranking; the benchmark section explains its limitations.

items.title: AI Agent Tool Use: MCP, CLI, Skills, and Code Execution
items.summary:
# AI Agent Tool Use: MCP, CLI, Skills, and Code Execution

This article is for engineers building agents that use tools. It compares JSON tool calling, MCP, CLI commands, and sandboxed code so you can choose an execution mechanism for your workload and use Skills to guide it.

**Skills** provide instructions for choosing and using tools. The **harness** is the ordinary program around the model: it builds prompts, checks a proposed call, runs an approved call, and decides when the task is done.

This third article in the series adds the action layer to [Part 1's reasoning loops](/blog/2026/01/31/ai-agent-reasoning-loops/) and [Part 2's memory](/blog/2026/02/14/ai-agent-memory-architecture/). [Part 4](/blog/2026/04/20/ai-agent-security/) examines the policy check before execution, and [Part 6](/blog/2026/07/22/ai-agent-harness-engineering/) examines the harness that runs both the call and that check.

The tooling story changed in 2025–2026. **MCP**, the Model Context Protocol, gave vendors one shared way to expose external services. Code-executing agents showed that a model can sometimes compose a small program more efficiently than it can issue a long sequence of JSON calls. Anthropic reported a **98.7% token reduction** for one Google Drive-to-Salesforce workflow, and the CodeAct paper reported task-success gains of up to **20 percentage points** across its benchmark setup. Those results describe their tasks and harnesses, not a universal advantage for code execution.

A later section applies Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) design principles to the [Market Analyst Agent](https://github.com/slavadubrov/market-analyst-agent), a small LangGraph research agent I built for Part 1 that fetches market data and writes an analyst report.

items.title: NER Guide 2026: GLiNER, spaCy, Transformers, and LLMs
items.summary:
# NER Guide 2026: GLiNER, spaCy, Transformers, and LLMs

This guide is for engineers choosing named entity recognition (NER) for retrieval, privacy, or document-processing pipelines. It explains how to choose between span recognizers and structured LLM extraction, evaluate their errors, and test deployment options against the latency and cost your workload permits.

NER turns text into labeled pieces that a program can use. Given “Bill Gates founded Microsoft on April 4, 1975,” it can return the contiguous text spans `Bill Gates`, `Microsoft`, and `April 4, 1975` with the types person, organization, and date. In a span-based encoder such as GLiNER, the model reads the text once and scores candidate spans against the labels you supply.

For a retrieval or privacy pipeline, I would first ask whether the output must be a literal mention. That decision separates a span recognizer from systems that also normalize values, link records, or infer facts. LLMs remain useful for proposing training annotations and handling cases that require inference or normalization.

> **Companion repo:** [**ner-field-guide**](https://github.com/slavadubrov/ner-field-guide) provides span scoring, GLiNER examples, reviewed annotation conversion, and ONNX comparisons. Its synthetic smoke checks are not a model ranking. Published benchmark results below remain separate from the companion's recorded experiments.

items.title: AI Agent Security: Permissions, Sandboxes, and MCP Threats
items.summary:
# AI Agent Security: Permissions, Sandboxes, and MCP Threats

This guide is for engineers building or deploying tool-using AI agents. It explains where to enforce tool permissions, sandbox restrictions, credential limits, and human approval, so you can decide which check stops an unsafe action before it reaches files, networks, or an external system.

The **harness** is the code that builds each prompt, decides which proposed tool calls run, and returns results to the model. Most checks belong there because it is the last cheap place to stop a command. After a command runs, the sandbox, the credentials it received, and any recovery process must contain the damage. Some incidents in this article never reach a model at all.

AI agent security is broader than LLM safety. Early guardrail products inspected the input and output of one model call. They could filter toxic text, redact personal data, block jailbreaks, and reject off-topic answers. That boundary was useful while the model could only return text.

Tool loops added filesystems, shells, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and credentials. That expanded the threat model from unsafe text to unsafe actions. The seven incident groups below span indirect prompt injection and failures in configuration, identity, and software distribution. Text screening can help with some malicious inputs; it cannot replace the controls at those execution boundaries.

When an agent can read a repository, call a tool, or send data to a third party, map every proposed action to the check that can stop it. The sections below cover permissions, hooks, sandboxes, credentials, and human review.

items.title: RAG Evaluation Metrics: Retrieval, Reranking, Generation
items.summary:
# RAG Evaluation Metrics: Retrieval, Reranking, Generation

For engineers operating or evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, this reference maps failures in document parsing, filtering, retrieval, reranking, and generation to the metric that identifies each one. It also shows which checks run before release and which monitor live traffic.

A RAG system with broken relevance filters can run for months without triggering an operational alert. It still returns answers and meets its latency target, but the answers rely on incomplete evidence. Recall@k against the original eligible gold set exposes the loss. Latency and availability dashboards do not.

items.title: Long-Running AI Agent Runtime: Sessions and Checkpoints
items.summary:
# Long-Running AI Agent Runtime: Sessions and Checkpoints

This guide is for engineers deploying tool-using AI agents that need to survive worker restarts. It explains where to keep session logs, checkpoints, tool execution, and traces, then compares deployment patterns so you can choose a recoverable runtime.

An agent run may last for hours, but its worker process can restart at any time. The runtime keeps the run's state, executes its tools, and recovers if a tool call stops halfway through. The model still chooses the next action. [Part 6](/blog/2026/07/22/ai-agent-harness-engineering/) covers the harness: the code that supplies context, checks tool calls, and decides whether the work is complete.

items.title: AI Agent Evaluation in Production: Traces to Test Suites
items.summary:
# AI Agent Evaluation in Production: Traces to Test Suites

This guide is for engineers evaluating tool-using AI agents in production. You will learn how to turn failed runs into repeatable tests, check the agent's actions as well as its answers, and use those tests before the next release.

items.title: Model Quantization Guide: Foundations to Production Serving
items.summary:
# Model Quantization Guide: Foundations to Production Serving

This quantization guide is for engineers deploying language models who need to
reduce memory use or improve serving speed. You will learn how to choose what
to compress, match a number format to your hardware and runtime, and compare
memory, latency, and output quality before deployment. It also covers
the separate checks needed for diffusion image models.

Quantization reduces the bits used for [weights, activations, or the KV cache](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/features/quantization.html).
**Weights** are the model parameters learned during training. **Activations** are
intermediate values computed from each input. The **key-value (KV) cache** keeps
values from earlier tokens for reuse during generation. Compressing weights can
make a model fit in GPU memory while leaving too little room for a long
conversation. The target you compress and the GPU code that executes it determine
which limit you relieve.

Start with what makes the request slow or too large. Processing the input prompt
is called **prefill**; generating the answer one token at a time is **decode**.
Prefill can be limited by GPU arithmetic, while decode can be limited by how fast
weights load from memory. Model weights and the growing KV cache can also exhaust
GPU memory. The first table maps these problems to possible fixes; later sections
explain the arithmetic and checks needed before deployment.

A lower bit-width is only a candidate. The decision needs both task-quality
results and serving measurements for the model, runtime, and traffic you will use.
The benchmarks here are published results from other teams; the companion
provides planning and evaluation commands, not evidence that your deployment
will achieve the same result.

items.title: Harness Engineering for AI Agents: Designing Control Loops
items.summary:
# Harness Engineering for AI Agents: Designing Control Loops

**Harness engineering** is the design of the control code around an agent's
reasoning loop. For engineers building or reviewing coding agents, this
article explains how to verify completion, retry safely, preserve progress
between sessions, and compare optional controls against a fixed baseline.

An agent can finish its turn while the work is still incomplete. For a coding
agent, the useful evidence is the changed artifact and its required test
results. A final message saying "done" does not establish either.

The **harness** supplies context, validates and authorizes tool calls,
records results, and decides whether the evidence is sufficient to accept
the work. The [runtime](/blog/2026/05/26/ai-agent-runtime/) keeps execution
and state alive underneath it. The store examples below are fictional;
the companion lab is a deterministic simulation, not a measurement of a
live agent.

items.title: Meta-engineering AI systems: from traces to better memory
items.summary:
# Meta-engineering AI systems: from traces to better memory

This article opens **Meta-Engineering AI Systems**, a six-part guide to **closed-loop AI engineering**: using agents to investigate failures, test changes, and use the results to improve AI systems.

An AI application's behavior depends on more than its model. Prompts, retrieved information, stored memory, tools, and application code all affect what happens. When an answer is wrong, several changes may look plausible. The engineering problem is deciding which change helps, what it costs, and what else it breaks.

I use **meta-engineering** here for designing the improvement process itself: what evidence the agent sees, what it may change, how we test its proposals, and who decides whether to adopt them. **Closed-loop** describes how that process learns from its experiments. Each result informs what we try or use next, including when a proposed change fails.

We can automate that work in stages. A person may specify the exact changes to test, define a set of permitted alternatives for a search algorithm, or delegate the next proposal to an LLM agent. The runner tests each candidate and preserves evidence for the next decision. This series focuses on bringing agents into that process while keeping execution, evaluation, and adoption under explicit control.

The question running through all six parts is how much of that work we can delegate to an agent while keeping the evidence and the decision to adopt a change trustworthy. We will start by mapping the whole system, then build a small working version around agent memory.

items.title: TypeScript for Python ML engineers: build an agent service
items.summary:
# TypeScript for Python ML engineers: build an agent service

Most TypeScript guides start with basic programming or front-end DOM work. This
guide starts with the Python service concepts that transfer and the runtime
behavior that does not, because the goal is a backend AI service.

The example is a streaming agent service for experienced Python ML and backend
engineers. It follows a request through validation, tool execution, HTTP
streaming, and persistence. The useful questions are concrete: what happens
when tool arguments arrive in fragments, a stream fails after HTTP 200, or a
worker claims the same job twice?

The code is in
[**slavadubrov/typescript-agent-service**](https://github.com/slavadubrov/typescript-agent-service).
It includes two agent-loop implementations, Postgres run history, a worker,
and an MCP server. You can run its offline demo without an API key, then use
the Python-to-TypeScript map below to read and modify the service. Heavy
numerics stay in Python; this guide covers orchestration, HTTP, and streaming.

items.title: MacBook Setup for AI Engineering: macOS Tools and Workflow
items.summary:
# MacBook Setup for AI Engineering: macOS Tools and Workflow

This is the setup I apply to a fresh MacBook before doing AI engineering work. It
covers the command-line tools macOS does not include, Homebrew, Python with uv,
the shell, terminal and editor choices, Docker, and local AI tools.

The useful boundary is between required foundations and personal preferences. Xcode
Command Line Tools, Homebrew, Git, and a Python workflow are foundations. Warp,
iTerm2, Powerlevel10k, Cursor, and local model runners are choices. The commands
below install the foundation; the later sections record the choices I make on top.
This is a documented setup sequence, not a bit-for-bit reproducible machine image.

items.title: LLM Engineering Guide: 45 Concepts for Production Systems
items.summary:
# LLM Engineering Guide: 45 Concepts for Production Systems

An LLM service can miss its latency SLO because decode is limited by memory bandwidth, because the KV cache has consumed the batch budget, or because the queue is masking both. A fine-tuning run can fail for a different version of the same reason: model state no longer fits the hardware. The right fix follows from the bottleneck, not from the longest list of techniques.

This is a reference for engineers who already know basic ML and systems concepts, and need to connect a production symptom to the relevant part of the stack. It covers 45 concepts across hardware, inference, training, deployment, applications, and operations. Use an entry to identify the mechanism, its practical consequence, and the condition that limits the cited result; then use the linked deep dive or your own benchmark to make the decision.

items.title: Open-Weight LLM Variants, Formats, and Quantization
items.summary:
# Open-Weight LLM Variants, Formats, and Quantization

Names such as `Model-32B-A3B-Instruct-AWQ` look dense because they combine several independent decisions: family and size, architecture, training role, and quantization. A repository may package those weights as sharded Safetensors, while a community conversion of the same checkpoint appears as `Q4_K_M.gguf`.

Those labels do not share one category: GPTQ and AWQ are quantization methods, GGUF is a container and runtime ecosystem, and MoE is an architecture. Reading the layers separately makes the download choice easier.

When choosing between a `Q4_K_M.gguf` download for local inference and an AWQ Safetensors repository for GPU serving, start with the checkpoint behavior and architecture your task needs. Then confirm that its numeric representation, package layout, and target runtime fit the available hardware, memory, and serving constraints.

items.title: MCP Server Tutorial: Build with Python, uv, and FastMCP
items.summary:
# MCP Server Tutorial: Build with Python, uv, and FastMCP

Python developers can turn a local feature-store workflow into a version-pinned FastMCP server for Claude Desktop, using **uv** to create the environment, expose tools and a resource, and verify the server locally before the desktop connection.

items.title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: Memory and Tools
items.summary:
# Context Engineering for AI Agents: Memory and Tools

Context engineering is the pipeline that selects what a model sees before each decision: instructions, examples, knowledge, memory, tool definitions, observations, and guardrails. An agent does not act on everything the system knows. It acts on the working set assembled for the next model call.

That selection is where many failures begin. A stale preference looks current. Retrieved text contains an instruction. A long tool result hides the failed precondition. A summary remembers the decision but loses which file changed.

For engineers building or operating AI agents, retrieval systems, and tool-using applications, the practical job is to assemble the smallest sufficient working set for each agent decision while preserving scope, provenance, and permissions. This article shows how to design a per-decision context pipeline, find its trust boundaries, test whether its working set supports the task, and make failures inspectable rather than blaming a model that only sees the assembled input.

items.title: LoRAX Serving Guide: LoRA Adapters on Kubernetes at Scale
items.summary:
# LoRAX Serving Guide: LoRA Adapters on Kubernetes at Scale

One base model and many LoRA adapters create an unusual serving problem. The base weights are shared, but every request may need a different set of adapter weights. A conventional one-deployment-per-variant design wastes GPU memory when most variants are idle.

[LoRAX](https://github.com/predibase/lorax) addresses that long tail. It loads adapters on demand, batches requests for different adapters, and moves adapter weights between GPU and CPU memory. The attractive headline is "thousands of fine-tuned models on one GPU." The engineering question is narrower: given your active adapter set, arrival pattern, and latency target, does exchange scheduling help enough to justify another serving runtime?

This guide is for inference and platform engineers who need to serve many LoRA variants from one base model. It shows how to test the documented APIs, size the working set, and turn the starter Helm chart into an explicit production plan.

items.title: Local LLMs on macOS: Ollama, LM Studio, MLX, llama.cpp
items.summary:
# Local LLMs on macOS: Ollama, LM Studio, MLX, llama.cpp

Engineers running local models on an Apple Silicon Mac need to size the complete workload, not just choose a model that downloads. Apple Silicon can run everyday prompts without a remote API because the CPU and GPU share one [unified memory pool](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/usage/unified_memory.html), but model weights compete there with the KV cache, runtime workspace, and macOS.

Once the intended model, context, and memory headroom fit, choose the control surface that matches the workflow: Ollama for a managed local service, LM Studio for desktop inspection, llama.cpp for direct GGUF execution, or MLX-LM for Apple-native Python. That keeps model-quality testing separate from tool choice and gives you a fair, memory-aware benchmark for the stack you will run.

items.title: AI Agent Memory: Schema-Guided State and Provenance
items.summary:
# AI Agent Memory: Schema-Guided State and Provenance

Long-running agents often retrieve stale facts because ordinary semantic memory has no rule for deciding which value is current.

When a user changes a passport deadline from July 15 to June 30, vector search can retrieve both statements. A stateful memory layer must record that the June 30 value supersedes the earlier one.

For engineers building long-running or multi-tenant agents, that stale-fact failure is why memory must survive separate runs while enforcing current state and tenant boundaries. The design below shows how to write typed records and test current versus point-in-time reads without treating vector recall as the source of truth.

items.title: uv on macOS: Managing Python Versions, Projects, and Tools
items.summary:
# uv on macOS: Managing Python Versions, Projects, and Tools

I switched my Python workflow to uv. It replaced the tool switching I used to do between pip, virtual environments, pip-tools, pipx, and project managers. One executable now covers most of that work.

The workflows are still different. For Python developers moving to uv on macOS from pip, virtual environments, pip-tools, or pipx, a project, an inline-metadata script, a one-off CLI, and an installed CLI each belong to a different environment and lifecycle. The commands below show how to choose among them.

## Quick start

```bash
# Install uv with Homebrew
brew install uv

# Start a project
uv init example-app
cd example-app
uv add httpx
uv run python main.py

# Run an isolated CLI without installing it permanently
uvx ruff check .
```

items.title: Scaling LLMs with Multi-GPU and Multi-Node Parallelism
items.summary:
# Scaling LLMs with Multi-GPU and Multi-Node Parallelism

Large-model workloads move beyond one GPU for different reasons. A training job may run out of memory on optimizer state. Another may run out on long-sequence activations. A model that fits may still miss its throughput target. Each problem calls for a different partition and communication pattern.

This is a practical walk-through of the main parallelism strategies and the constraints behind them, informed by Hugging Face's [Ultra-Scale Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nanotron/ultrascale-playbook). The goal is to show what each split buys, what it communicates, and when combinations become necessary.

items.title: MLOps vs LLMOps: Infrastructure for Foundation Models
items.summary:
# MLOps vs LLMOps: Infrastructure for Foundation Models

When a foundation-model release regresses, the weight file may be unchanged: a prompt, retrieval index, tool permission, route, or policy can be the moving part. For ML, platform, and AI application engineers who already operate conventional MLOps, the practical artifact is therefore a release manifest that names those dependencies and points to the first control to inspect when a failure appears.

This is an editorial operating model, not a claim that every application needs the same platform. Keep MLOps lineage, staged delivery, monitoring, and rollback; expand the unit you version when generated answers or tool actions make behavior depend on more than the weights.

items.title: Zsh Startup Files: .zprofile vs .zshrc on macOS and Linux
items.summary:
# Zsh Startup Files: .zprofile vs .zshrc on macOS and Linux

If your terminal feels slow, or an environment variable appears in one terminal but not another, the cause is often Zsh's startup mode. The two files most people reach for are `~/.zprofile` and `~/.zshrc`, but neither filename alone tells you whether a line belongs there.

Zsh chooses startup files from two independent properties: whether the shell is a **login shell** and whether it is **interactive**. Terminal applications on macOS and Linux can choose different combinations, so inspect the running shell instead of assuming the operating system decides for you.

items.title: pyproject.toml Guide: Packaging, Dependencies, and Tools
items.summary:
# pyproject.toml Guide: Packaging, Dependencies, and Tools

Older Python projects often spread configuration across `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, requirements files, `MANIFEST.in`, and separate files for development tools. `pyproject.toml` gives those concerns a common home, although it does not replace every project file or make every section part of one standard.

This guide walks through the file from build configuration to project metadata and tool settings. Four owners keep the sections distinct: what builds the project, what the project publishes, what contributors need locally, and what individual tools configure.

items.title: Stable Diffusion on macOS: Local Image Tools Compared
items.summary:
# Stable Diffusion on macOS: Local Image Tools Compared

Running image models locally on macOS is mostly a tooling choice. Draw Things, DiffusionBee, ComfyUI, AUTOMATIC1111, and Fooocus overlap, but they differ in setup, model support, workflow control, extensions, and automation.

A drag-and-drop app gets you started quickly; a node graph takes longer to learn but exposes more of the pipeline. On Apple Silicon, the application, model family, precision, image size, and workflow all affect whether generation fits in memory. Choose the interface from the work you need to reproduce, then test the exact model and settings.

items.title: Enterprise RAG Challenge 3: Lessons from Public Entries
items.summary:
# Enterprise RAG Challenge 3: Lessons from Public Entries

Enterprise RAG Challenge 3 (ERC3) asked agents to complete business tasks against a simulated company API. The frozen prize leaderboard is unusually useful because many entrants published more than a score: architecture, model mix, cost, and failure notes.

I reviewed those public descriptions to answer a narrower question: which design choices recurred in strong submissions, and which of them are useful outside this benchmark?

By the end, you should be able to turn these observations into design hypotheses for your own agent traces, then test them against your task mix and failure costs.

items.title: DeepSeek mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
items.summary:
# DeepSeek mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections

Modern deep learning rests on the residual connection. Hyper-Connections (HC) explore another architectural dimension: widen the residual state into several interacting streams. DeepSeek's **[Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880)** paper studies how to keep that routing stable at larger training scales.

This post starts with standard residual connections, then adds Hyper-Connections and the instability they create. The mHC constraint and its implementation cost come at the end.
